To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a single demonstration of a multi-stage task can be used to train a hierarchical policy that is capable of generalizing to new objects and (ii) the hierarchical policy can be trained with only a single demonstration of the full task, and a small number of demonstrations for each of the primitive skills.
we propose a novel approach to learning hierarchical imitation learning of compound visuomotor tasks from a single video demonstration of the full task.
we can learn to perform compound tasks with novel objects from a single video demonstration of the task, and that we can do so with a small number of parameters and a small amount of training data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: “Can a robot learn a complex task by watching a human perform that task only once?”
the problem of learning to perform multi-stage visuomotor tasks from a single video demonstration of a human.
the following problem: How do we learn a hierarchical policy that can perform a multi-stage task from one video of a human demonstrator?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we present a novel method for learning to perform multi-stage visuomotor tasks by watching a human demonstrator perform the task once.
we propose a method to learn multi-stage tasks from video demonstrations, which can be applied to novel object instances, and we show that our approach is effective in simulation and on a real robot.
our work is the first to demonstrate hierarchical imitation learning with a single video demonstration, while also using raw pixels and novel objects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are proposing a new paradigm in imitation learning, where the agent can learn to perform a new task by observing a human demonstration of a new task.
we propose a method for learning multi-stage vision tasks by “watch a human do the task once, and then do the task yourself.”
we are learning a policy for learning a policy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a hierarchical approach to imitation learning can enable learning of multi-stage tasks from a single video demonstration, while leveraging demonstration videos of sub-tasks.

it is possible for a robot to acquire complex multi-stage behaviors from a single video demonstration by learning to learn primitive behaviors, and then composing these behaviors to solve compound tasks.
we can learn a diverse set of multi-stage tasks with novel objects from a single video demonstration.
